A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Scam2Prompt and Innoc2Scam-bench. All 30 pages of v2 and 36 pages of v3, including appendices, are readable and support comparison. Relocated sections, figures, tables, and examples can be matched.

before.justification: v2 reports original large-scale code-generation audits, seven-model benchmark evaluations, creative-sampling experiments, and NeMo guardrail results.

after.justification: v3 retains the original audit and reports revised benchmark results plus additional model-size, prompt-pattern, moderation, and retrieval-augmented experiments.

M1.justification: The core Scam2Prompt procedure retains its crawler, prompt-synthesis and code-generation templates, URL extraction, three-detector oracle, and majority-vote human validation. Benchmark curation changes and added defense comparisons do not establish a redesign of this auditing algorithm.

E1.justification: The seed databases and broad Web3/non-Web3 coverage remain. v3 narrows benchmark tasks by excluding summarization and manual-workflow requests (Appendix D.1), and adds a search-enabled code-generation scenario (Appendix I.2). The newly reported domain breakdown characterizes existing coverage rather than adding domains.

E2.justification: v2's defense evaluation uses NeMo Guardrails with Llama Nemotron Safety Guard V2. v3 retains this comparator and adds OpenAI Moderation API, Llama Guard 3, and GPT-4o with search and URL-safety self-checking. These substantially broaden the evaluated defenses; Guardrails AI is discussed but not included in a reported comparison.

E3.justification: Benchmark construction now classifies and samples before human validation, producing 1,377 prompts instead of 1,559. v3 adds completion-conditioned and refusal metrics, a comparison restricted to 637 jointly completed prompts, and controlled Gemma-size, prompt-template, and retrieval settings. These materially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v3 adds model-size and task-capability diagnostics, decomposition/few-shot sensitivity tests, shared-completion analyses, benchmark domain characterization, and analysis of newly generated endpoints and retrieval failures. The earlier creative-sampling experiment, overlap analysis, and running examples remain; their relocation is not additional evidence.

E5.justification: Appendix F introduces 95% Wald confidence intervals and paired McNemar tests over both the full benchmark and shared completions; v2 reports neither. These quantify uncertainty across prompts, without establishing additional repeated runs. v2's explicit prompt-hash seed rule is also absent from v3.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces results on 1,559 prompts with results on 1,377: Gemini-2.5-Pro changes from 198/1,559 (12.7%) to 178/1,377 (12.9%), and DeepSeek-Chat-V3.1 from 683/1,559 (43.8%) to 651/1,377 (47.3%). These are different-benchmark results, not same-setting deterioration. New results include GPT-4o's 50.04% versus 29.41% malicious rates without versus with search/self-checking. The initial audit and creative-sampling results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3 retains the same oracle-based problem and objective, with prompt-category labels changed to developer-style/non-developer-style. Neither version supplies theoretical results or proofs about the framework. The added standard statistical tests concern evaluation rather than new theoretical development.

C1.justification: The central claims about malicious endpoint generation, automated auditing, and benchmark transfer remain. v3 adds an explicit defense-evaluation contribution and extends the inadequate-defense claim from guardrails to retrieval-augmented agents, emphasizing explicit URL-oracle checking.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly distinguishes stress-test rates from natural developer-prompt incidence and develops the interpretation of refusal-conditioned comparisons. It adds substantive discussion of oracle errors, unavailable alignment details, smaller-model capability confounds, possible deployed-model updates, and retrieval failure mechanisms, substantially expanding qualifications and explanations.

D1.justification: v3 documents exclusion criteria and examples, domain-labeling heuristics, additional guardrail identifiers, alternate templates, experiment dates, search-plugin configuration, and revised code/data access locations. However, v2's prompt-generation temperature of 0.3 and prompt-hash seed instructions disappear, and the new few-shot examples are omitted from the PDF.

R1.justification: Related work expands to distinguish passive auditing from code-poisoning attacks such as TrojanPuzzle and You Autocomplete Me, and from CWE-based benchmarks including SecCodePLT and SafeGenBench. Added guardrail, unlearning, and data-cleaning literature further broadens the paper's positioning beyond v2's treatment.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the document: dataset construction moves from the main text to Appendix D, appendices are regrouped, and Discussion and Impact Statement sections are added. It also revises terminology throughout, edits the introductory narrative, and considerably shortens the displayed code examples.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to predominantly two-column layout. Figure 3 is redrawn, the separate dataset-construction diagram is removed, Table 2 gains conditional-rate columns, and new statistical matrices, hierarchy figures, experiment tables, and prompt boxes are introduced. Existing figures and listings are extensively relocated and reformatted.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens benchmark validity by excluding non-coding requests and clarifying that reported rates describe a stress test. Uncertainty estimates, shared-completion comparisons, and broader robustness and defense evaluations address important weaknesses in v2's evidence. These gains outweigh lost sampling disclosures and reporting defects, including the moderation denominator of 3,452 versus 3,441 outputs in Table 2, and Figure 9's grouping of Claude despite significant differences in Table 10.
